source: Fleming and Lau (2014) How to measure metacognition
finding: Splits confidence quality into three separate things: bias (overall level of confidence), sensitivity (how well confidence separates correct from incorrect trials) and efficiency (sensitivity relative to task performance).
numbers: No single number. Bias = share of high-confidence trials or mean rating. Sensitivity = separation of the two type-2 distributions. Efficiency = meta-d'/d'.
quote: Metacognitive sensitivity is the separation between the distributions
limits: Review, not new data. Cartoon distributions are not meant to be Gaussian.
agent_relevance: Our agent must report these separately: how sure it is (bias), whether sure answers are the right ones (sensitivity), and how good that is for the skill level (efficiency).

source: Fleming and Lau (2014) How to measure metacognition (correlation measures)
finding: Phi and Goodman-Kruskal gamma, long the standard in memory metacognition, are contaminated by response bias. They cannot tell a good monitor from one that just says 'high' often.
numbers: Gamma advocated by Nelson (1984); Masson and Rotello (2009) showed gamma bias. No pooled numbers in this review.
limits: The review cites the gamma critique; the original simulations were not read.
agent_relevance: Do not score our agent's confidence with a plain correlation. Use AUROC or a proper score.

source: Fleming and Lau (2014) How to measure metacognition (type-2 AUROC)
finding: Type-2 AUROC (area under the curve of confidence for correct versus incorrect trials) is bias-free and needs no Gaussian assumption. Type-2 d' = z(H2) - z(FA2) assumes equal-variance Gaussians that Galvin et al. (2003) showed are false.
numbers: AUROC2 = 0.5 is chance. H2 = P(high conf | correct); FA2 = P(high conf | incorrect).
limits: AUROC2 still scales with task accuracy, so it cannot compare skills at different difficulty.
agent_relevance: This is the exact metric used by LLM papers (Kuhn, Xiong, Tian). Use AUROC for sample-agreement scores.

source: Fleming and Lau (2014) How to measure metacognition (meta-d' and efficiency)
finding: meta-d' is the d' that an ideal observer would need to produce the observed confidence data. Efficiency is meta-d'/d'. A value of 1 is ideal; 0.7 means 30 percent of the evidence is lost when making confidence judgments.
numbers: meta-d'/d' = 1 ideal; 0.7 example; meta-d' - d' is the difference version (Rounis 2010); log of the ratio recommended when d' is small.
quote: A meta-d'/d' value of 1 indicates a theoretically ideal value of metacognitive efficiency
limits: meta-d' cannot tell criterion noise from extra rating noise. The ratio is unstable when d' is near 0.
agent_relevance: Gives a way to compare confidence quality across tasks of different difficulty for our agent.

source: Fleming and Lau (2014) How to measure metacognition (SDRM alternative)
finding: The Stochastic Detection and Retrieval Model (Jang et al. 2012) draws two evidence samples per item, one for the decision and one for confidence, correlated by rho. It separates sampling correlation from noise in the confidence criteria.
numbers: Parameters: correlation rho between the two samples; trial-to-trial variance of confidence criteria.
limits: Requires heavy interpretation of fitted parameters; the review prefers meta-d' for simplicity.
agent_relevance: Same idea as sampling twice from one model: if the two samples share the same errors (high rho), confidence cannot help. Links to guardrail G4.

source: Fleming and Lau (2014) How to measure metacognition (Dunning-Kruger reading)
finding: The Dunning-Kruger pattern has two readings. Low performers rate noisily just because type-1 d' is low (a sensitivity effect), or skill and efficiency share resources. One-shot self ratings cannot separate bias, sensitivity and efficiency.
numbers: Cites Kruger and Dunning (1999): worst performers showed the largest gap between actual performance and a one-shot rating.
limits: Trial-by-trial efficiency data are needed to decide; none given here.
agent_relevance: When our agent fails on a hard item, weak confidence there is expected from the maths, not proof of poor self-knowledge.

source: Fleming and Lau (2014) How to measure metacognition (efficiency across groups)
finding: Efficiency lets us compare groups and domains with unmatched accuracy: vision versus memory, patients versus controls, adolescents versus adults, species.
numbers: Weil et al. (2013): efficiency rises during adolescence. Review gives no effect sizes.
limits: Cross-domain generality claims rest on a few studies of the time (Baird 2013, McCurdy 2013).
agent_relevance: Suggests testing the agent's confidence quality per task type, not as one global number.

source: Galvin, Podd, Drga and Whitmore (2003) Type 2 tasks in the theory of signal detectability
finding: Showed that if type-1 evidence is equal-variance Gaussian, the type-2 distributions of correct and incorrect trials are unequal in variance and non-Gaussian. This is the base of meta-d'.
numbers: Numbers not read; cited in Fleming and Lau (2014).
limits: Not opened; known only via the 2014 review.
agent_relevance: Explains why simple type-2 d' is wrong and AUROC is safer for our confidence from agreement.

source: Maniscalco and Lau (2012) A signal detection theoretic approach for estimating metacognitive sensitivity from confidence ratings
finding: Introduced meta-d' and the M-ratio (meta-d'/d'): fit the type-1 SDT model to type-2 data to find the sensitivity that would explain the confidence ratings, in the same units as d'.
numbers: No numbers read this session.
limits: Not opened (only the 2014 review description was read). Requires multi-level confidence ratings and a decent trial count.
agent_relevance: Template for scoring how much of the model's own decision evidence reaches its confidence.

source: Nelson (1984) A comparison of current measures of the accuracy of feeling-of-knowing predictions
finding: Argued for gamma because it does not assume SDT distributions and wanted metacognition measures independent of memory ability (logical independence).
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened; later shown to be contaminated by bias (Masson and Rotello 2009).
agent_relevance: Origin of the demand that confidence quality be independent of accuracy.

source: Masson and Rotello (2009) Sources of bias in the Goodman-Kruskal gamma coefficient
finding: Showed gamma can give biased estimates of metacognitive accuracy because it depends on bias and on the underlying evidence distributions.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened; cited in Fleming and Lau (2014).
agent_relevance: Another reason to avoid gamma-type scores in our evaluation.

source: Koriat (2012) The self-consistency model of subjective confidence
finding: Confidence is a sampling process: the person draws a few representations of the answer and confidence reflects how much they agree. Confidence thus tracks consistency across samples, not the strength of the chosen answer's evidence.
numbers: Exact numbers not read.
limits: Not opened; recalled from the literature, so not verified this session. Limit by design: consistency cannot beat the accuracy of the sampled pool.
agent_relevance: The core human precedent for 'confidence from consistency of samples, by code'.

source: Koriat (2008) Subjective confidence in one's answers: the consensuality principle
finding: For general-knowledge questions, confidence is higher when the answer is one most people choose, so confidence tracks consensus, not truth. For consensually wrong items, confidence is high and wrong.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened; recalled, not verified.
agent_relevance: Warning: agreement among samples from one model is a consensus; if the model's modal answer is wrong, agreement misleads (G4).

source: Koriat (1997) Monitoring one's own knowledge during study: a cue-utilization approach
finding: Judgments of learning rely on cues such as ease of processing, not on direct access to memory strength.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened; recalled.
agent_relevance: People's confidence is inferential; likewise our agent's confidence should be computed from cues we can count.

source: Wang et al. (2022) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning in language models
finding: Sample many reasoning paths and take the most common final answer. Gains over greedy chain-of-thought on arithmetic and commonsense tasks. The share of samples agreeing with the final answer is highly correlated with accuracy on GSM8K, so it serves as an uncertainty estimate.
numbers: Absolute gains: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-challenge +3.9 (PaLM-540B or GPT-3).
quote: one can use low consistency as an indicator that the model has low confidence
limits: The correlation is shown in a figure on GSM8K; no calibration error reported in the text read.
agent_relevance: Direct basis for confidence from consistency of samples. Agreement share is the cheap signal.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple-choice when options are lettered, and calibration improves with size. They can judge their own samples with P(True); showing the model many of its own samples first improves this. They can be trained to predict P(IK).
numbers: Models up to 52B. Few-shot self-evaluation is well calibrated; zero-shot less so. P(IK) trained on TriviaQA separates well but is poorly calibrated on new tasks. Larger k mainly improves calibration, not AUROC.
quote: Models can self-evaluate whether their own samples are True or False, though this tends to be a more challenging task
limits: Calibration is worse zero-shot and out of distribution; models find their own samples more plausible.
agent_relevance: P(True) on its own sample is weak. Seeing other samples first helps, which matches an agreement-based design.

source: Lin, Hilton and Evans (2022) Teaching models to express their uncertainty in words
finding: GPT-3 finetuned to say a confidence in words (CalibratedMath) is calibrated in distribution and moderately under distribution shift. It is not just copying human wording nor reading its own logits.
numbers: Finetuned on Add-subtract, tested on Multi-answer and Multiply-divide, scored by MSE and mean absolute deviation (MAD) against a constant baseline. Calibrated versions beat the baseline under shift; the exact table cells were garbled in text extraction so are not recorded.
limits: Fine-tuned GPT-3 only; arithmetic-style tasks; table cells unreadable here.
agent_relevance: Verbalized confidence can be trained, but we do not train. For a scaffold, prefer counted agreement over verbalized numbers.

source: Xiong et al. (2023) Can LLMs express their uncertainty? An empirical evaluation of confidence elicitation
finding: Verbalized confidence is overconfident. Calibration and failure prediction improve with model size, but even GPT-4 is near chance at separating right from wrong. Consistency over several samples beats verbalized confidence.
numbers: Vanilla verbalized: average ECE above 0.377 for GPT-3, Vicuna, GPT-3.5; GPT-4 average AUROC 62.7 percent. 5 samples with consistency raised GSM8K AUROC from 54.8 to 92.7 percent. Black-box versus white-box gap: 0.522 vs 0.605 AUROC. About 22.2 percent AUROC gain from GPT-3 to GPT-4.
quote: none of these techniques consistently outperform others
limits: No single strategy wins everywhere; all methods weak on professional-knowledge tasks (e.g., law).
agent_relevance: Strongest direct evidence for our design: same model, sampled agreement, computed by code, beats asking for a confidence number, especially on arithmetic.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just ask for calibration
finding: For RLHF chat models, verbalized confidence is often better calibrated than the token probabilities. Asking for several guesses with probabilities before the confidence helps further.
numbers: ECE cut by over 50 percent relative on TriviaQA, SciQ, TruthfulQA. ChatGPT TriviaQA: label prob ECE 0.140, AUC 0.869; verbalized 1-stage top-2 ECE 0.050, AUC 0.894. TruthfulQA: label prob AUC 0.418; verbalized top-1 AUC 0.545 (ECE 0.389).
quote: a system that guesses randomly and outputs 50% confidence each time has perfect ECE
limits: gpt-3.5-turbo (June 2023), GPT-4 and Claude 2; ECE alone is blind to discrimination; a flat 50 percent output has perfect binary ECE (the paper's own caveat).
agent_relevance: Contradicts Xiong on how bad verbalized confidence is; the answer depends on model and dataset. Always report AUROC next to ECE.

source: Kuhn, Gal and Farquhar (2023) Semantic uncertainty
finding: Entropy over meaning classes (sampled answers grouped by whether they mean the same) predicts correctness better than entropy of token sequences, lexical similarity or p(True).
numbers: TriviaQA and CoQA with OPT up to 30B. Semantic entropy AUROC beats predictive entropy, length-normalised entropy, lexical similarity; advantage grows with model size and number of samples; temperature has an intermediate optimum. Gain over p(True) is large.
limits: Open-source OPT; entailment checks to group answers; AUROC values read only from figures.
agent_relevance: Do the grouping in code (normalise final answers) and count classes: same as agreement but robust to paraphrase.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What large language models know and what people think they know
finding: People over-trust default LLM explanations; longer explanations raise human confidence without raising accuracy. Matching explanation wording to the model's internal confidence narrows both gaps.
numbers: 301 participants. Model AUC about 0.75 (GPT-3.5 .751, PaLM2 .746) and 0.781 (GPT-4o short answer); human AUC 0.589, 0.602, 0.592 on default explanations; mean human AUC 0.54 and 0.57 for long and short explanations.
limits: Prolific, native English, US; mixed multiple-choice and short-answer questions.
agent_relevance: Length is a confidence cue for human readers, as it is for LLM judges; a length-normalised report is safer (G5).

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large language models must be taught to know what they don't know
finding: Prompting alone is insufficient for calibration. Fine-tuning with LoRA on about 1000 graded examples beats baselines, and models can estimate other models' uncertainty.
numbers: About 1000 labelled examples suffice; 20,000 only slightly better; evaluated on MMLU multiple-choice and open-ended; includes a human-AI user study.
limits: Open-source models; requires labelled grading data.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a learned correctness probe is cheap, but we do not train.

source: Leng et al. (2025) Taming overconfidence in LLMs: reward calibration in RLHF
finding: RLHF reward models favour high stated confidence regardless of quality, which makes chat models verbally overconfident. Calibrated reward variants cut ECE without losing accuracy.
numbers: PPO-M and PPO-C on Llama3-8B and Mistral-7B, 6 datasets; one reported change: ECE down 6.44 points and accuracy up 2.73 on GSM8K; calibrated DPO reduced ECE by over 50 percent in one table.
limits: Small open models; reward-model fixes are training-time only.
agent_relevance: Explains why chat models say high confidence too often; another reason not to trust their own verbalised numbers.

source: Ji-An et al. (2025) Language models are capable of metacognitive monitoring and control of their internal activations
finding: A neurofeedback-style test shows LLMs can report and control only a small set of their activation directions; ability depends on number of in-context examples, interpretability of the direction and its explained variance.
numbers: Reporting accuracy measured against number of in-context examples; the reportable space has far lower dimension than the full activation space.
limits: Probe-based setup on open models; exact accuracy values not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Limits what an LLM can truthfully say about its own state; supports external counts over self-report.

source: Guo et al. (2017) On calibration of modern neural networks
finding: Modern networks are overconfident, and a single temperature scalar on the logits fixes calibration on held-out data (the temperature scaling used as ECE-t in Tian et al.).
numbers: Not opened for this line; cited in Tian et al.
limits: Not opened by me.
agent_relevance: A cheap post-hoc fix can calibrate agreement scores on a small held-out set.
